graduation_requirements.raw_text: Graduation Requirements .0 English 4 3.0 Mathematics 1.0 Fine Arts 3.5 Global Citizenship 1.0 Physical Education 8.0 Additional Credits (from any other areas) 3.0 Science 0.5 Health 40 Hours Community Service All Stowe High School students must earn the 24 credits listed to graduate: Yearly Course Registration Expectation s Grade Level Credit Registration Expectations 9th Grade 8 10th Grade 8 11th Grade 8 12th Grade 6 For students in grades 9-11, their course load of 8 classes may include one Raider Academic Block (RAB). However, students are always encouraged to carry academic courses that are rigorous and electives that match their interests in order to develop a full schedule. *Students who are participating in flexible pathways options or are supported by plans may carry different credit loads. Students are responsible for keeping track of their credits. Students should check-in with their advisor, school counselor and/or registrar if there are any questions about credits earned. A good practice to follow is to check credits at the start of every school year. While SHS faculty/staff will make their best effort to help students stay on track to graduate, credit checking and verification is the student's responsibility. *Students successfully completing Algebra 1 and/or World Language in middle school do NOT earn high school credits towards graduation. Courses taken in middle school, even if they are high school-level, will not count for high school credit and will not be included on the official Stowe High School transcript. Project Anagnorisis A four-year journey of self-discovery and of celebration of your progress through Stowe High School, is required for graduation. (see page 7) Community Service Requirement All students at Stowe High School must complete 40 hours of community service for graduation . Community service is an opportunity for all students to give back for the benefit of the community. We value the development of skills that enable students to be actively engaged citizens in any community. We require that students complete a minimum of 10 hours of community service each year of high school. Students can start accumulating service hours the summer before the start of their 9th grade year through May of their 12th grade year at SHS. Students must complete the SHS Community Service form to document their hours. All forms must be submitted in order for the hours to be recorded and applied to this graduation requirement. Forms are due no later than the last day of school for the current year. Students who do not complete their required 40 hours of service will not be eligible to graduate . Students generally complete community service hours through volunteer work opportunities for non-profit organizations within the Stowe community. Students can not get paid for their work nor can they earn hours for a position that is typically a paid role. 4

courses.description: This course, which satisfies the 9th grade English requirement, considers a variety of classic and contemporary texts. Students respond to their reading with argumentative writing that includes relevant evidence and analysis. Emphasis will be placed on the drafting and revision process. Students will practice speaking and listening skills through a variety of projects from discussions to dramatic performances of poems and speeches.

This course, which satisfies the 10 th grade English requirement, considers a variety of classic and contemporary texts. Students will continue to develop their narrative and argumentative writing skills. Speaking and listening are practiced through discussions and more formal recitations.
courses.prerequisites: English 9

courses.description: This course, which satisfies the 11 th grade English requirement, considers a variety of American classic and contemporary fiction, non-fiction, drama, short stories and poetry. Students will continue to demonstrate argumentative writing skills, including the revision process. Speaking and active listening will be practiced through discussions and more formal speaking opportunities.
courses.prerequisites: English 10

courses.description: The focus and content of this course, which satisfies the 12th grade English requirement, will shift markedly by semester. In semester 1, emphasis will be placed on personal essays that conform to the prescriptions of the Common Application, although students may tailor their work for alternative purposes. Time will be devoted to developing college-level vocabulary and designing creative projects that employ that vocabulary. College-level research tools will also be introduced. Semester 2 will be more differentiated; students will be able to propose and pursue their own projects, so long as they demonstrate critical reading and writing skills in these pursuits. Conceptually, the course will pose questions about trends in popular culture and our individual responsibilities therein. Throughout the year, we will examine literature and film dealing with this theme.
courses.prerequisites: English 11 or AP Literature and Composition

courses.description: This course is an intensive study of works judged by the College Board to be of literary merit. Students study literary terms and devices, and their applications. Particular emphasis is placed on thesis-driven evidence-based essay writing. Test taking strategies are also provided. This course may be taken in lieu of English 11 or English 12
courses.prerequisites: English 10
courses.fulfills_text: Credit Type: English; This course may be taken in lieu of English 11 or English 12

courses.description: This course is designed to offer students the opportunity to explore the world of creative writing in general and to focus on their personal goals as well. Over the course of the semester we will read and write in the three main forms of creative writing: Fiction, Poetry, and Drama. There will also be opportunities to explore other mediums such as songwriting, graphic novels, etc. We will look for opportunities for submitting student work for publication where appropriate.

This course will explore the crossroads of film and literature. Students will view both classic and contemporary films from a variety of genres and then analyze them from a literary standpoint. We will examine filmmaking choices, critical responses, and their social and cultural ramifications. Students will learn to use the extended vocabulary of literary analysis to explore issues such as identity, gender, and conflict and develop essential understandings about fiction, character development, society, and the art of storytelling.

This course helps students develop essential communication skills for speaking confidently in front of an audience. Through regular in-class practice, students will learn to organize and deliver effective speeches, including persuasive, informative, and impromptu types. Key topics include voice projection, body language, audience engagement, and overcoming stage fright. Students will also explore techniques for researching and crafting speeches, as well as receiving constructive feedback to improve their delivery. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to speak with clarity and confidence in a variety of settings, from classroom presentations to future public speaking opportunities.

This is a class designed to provide support and instruction to students who are developing their literacy skills. Students access this course through SHS faculty recommendation. This class can be taken multiple times.
courses.prerequisites: Students are not able to individually register for this course but will be scheduled for the course based upon teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Students are not able to individually register; scheduled by teacher recommendation.

courses.description: Graphic Design, Level I: Designed to teach the students the fundamental operational and mechanical skills necessary for working in the Adobe Photoshop Program. Students learn how to develop an eye for design and investigate the essential organizational skills required to work in Adobe Photoshop. Students gain an understanding of graphic images through customary projects grounded in compositional study and layout design, and begin to recognize the importance and use of symbolic meaning in graphic art form[s]. Students learn to use cameras, manipulate and edit photographic imagery to create graphic design.

Graphic Design Level II: Designed to teach the students the fundamental operational and mechanical skills necessary for working in the Adobe Illustrator Program. The class is structured to introduce students to the advertising section of the Graphic Design Program. Students learn how to develop an eye for design and investigate the essential organizational skills required to work in Adobe Illustrator. Students gain an understanding of graphic images through customary projects grounded in compositional study and layout design, and further recognize the importance of symbolic meaning through studying the history of logo design.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of the prior level

courses.description: Graphic Design Level III: Designed to teach the students the fundamental operational and mechanical skills necessary for working simultaneously in both Adobe programs, Photoshop and Illustrator. The class is structured to introduce students to the illustrative section of graphic images and to teach the students how to combine the two programs to achieve quality illustrations. The students learn how to develop an eye for design and investigate the essential organizational skills while being trained in both Adobe Programs, Photoshop and Illustrator. Students gain an understanding of the illustrative portion of Graphic Design Program through customary projects grounded in rendering techniques to effectively generate self-portraits, expressive caricatures, and book illustrations and graphic novels.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of the prior level

courses.description: Graphic Design Level IV: Designed to further a student who is seriously interested in Graphic Design. The student works on independent projects that will further the students technical and visual design skills in both Adobe programs, Photoshop and Illustrator. The class is structured to introduce students to the commercial section of graphic images. The students learn how to develop an eye for design and investigate the essential organizational skills while being trained in-both Adobe Programs, Photoshop and Illustrator. Students gain an understanding of the commercial portion of graphic images through customary projects grounded in package design and other technically complex projects. Students develop package designs for products and learn about the visual and symbolic prerequisites for selling a product.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of the prior level

courses.description: In Ceramics I, students will explore the creative and technical aspects of clay through handbuilding techniques and ceramic design application. This introductory course provides a foundation in the art of ceramics, encouraging students to experiment with form, texture, and design while developing a deeper understanding of the materials and processes involved in creating pottery and sculptural works. Throughout the semester, students will learn to manipulate clay through methods such as pinch pots, coils, and slabs. Emphasis will be placed on developing fine motor skills, artistic expression, and craftsmanship. Students will also explore various glazing and surface design techniques in order to bring their clay creations to life with color and texture.

Ceramics II, III, and IV is designed for students who have developed a foundational understanding of clay and wish to deepen their skills and explore their artistic voice in a more self-directed environment. Building on techniques learned in Ceramics I, these classes emphasize independent work, creative exploration, and the development of a personal style. Students will be encouraged to push their technical and artistic boundaries through a variety of handbuilding and wheel throwing techniques, with an increased focus on refinement, complexity, and innovation. Throughout these courses, students will have the opportunity to work on individual projects, setting their own goals and exploring ideas that reflect their unique interests and artistic vision. Emphasis will be placed on self-direction, allowing students to take ownership of their creative process while continuing to grow in technical proficiency and confidence. In addition to mastering advanced ceramic techniques, students will engage in critical self-reflection, peer critiques, and group discussions to foster a collaborative environment that supports artistic growth. Success in this course requires students to practice studio habits such as knowledge and care for tools and materials, work completion, time management and contributing to the cleanliness and safety of the studio space.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of the prior level

Weekly sketchbook drawing assignments, discussion and critique of art are an integral part of this course. Each semester students will practice the art of seeing by using both digital and analog cameras. A variety of assignments will develop visual awareness and open doors to using the camera in new ways. With permission, students will have the opportunity to leave campus with the school’s digital cameras. Students will learn to develop 35mm black and white film and use the darkroom to enlarge and make prints from their film negatives. There are 35 mm school cameras available for students to sign out and use in and outside of school. Camera handling and image improvement are learned in both media with darkroom techniques and the Adobe Photoshop program. Students should expect to spend time outside of school taking photos for assignments. Success in this course requires students to practice studio habits such as knowledge and care for tools and materials, work completion, time management and contributing to the cleanliness and safety of the studio space.

courses.description: During this semester course, students will delve into the dynamic world of mixed-media art, exploring various techniques and materials to expand their creative practice. The course will cover an array of mediums, including printmaking, screenprinting, bookmaking, collage, and experimental assemblage. Students will have the opportunity to combine 2D and 3D elements, pushing the boundaries of traditional art forms. Emphasis will be placed on personal expression and hands-on experimentation, encouraging students to integrate different materials and processes to create unique works of art. By the end of the course, students will have developed a broader understanding of how to merge various techniques into cohesive, innovative pieces . In addition to the exploration of new media, students will engage in critical self-reflection, peer critiques, and group discussions to foster a collaborative environment that supports artistic growth. Success in this course requires students to practice studio habits such as knowledge and care for tools and materials, work completion, time management and contributing to the cleanliness and safety of the studio space.

World History 9 is an examination of history from early humans to approximately 1800. It explores the themes of trade, empire building, belief system creation, and expansion. The course's foundation is historical study and therefore dedicates significant time to analysis and evaluation of primary and secondary sources as well as other methodologies of academic history. Students will demonstrate their learning in diverse ways, with a strong foundation in writing and discussion skills.

19th and 20th Century World History explores the ideas and events that got the world to where it is today. The course engages in deep dives into topics such as the French and Industrial Revolutions, Imperialism, Nationalism, and modern developments in the 20th century. The course will dedicate significant time to analysis and evaluation of primary and secondary sources as well as other methodologies of academic history. Students will demonstrate their learning in diverse ways, with a strong foundation in writing and discussion skills. The course culminates in a student driven project that focuses on Inquiry, Research & Communication skills.
courses.prerequisites: World History 9

courses.description: Students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes from 1200 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical connections; and utilizing reasoning about comparison, causation, and continuity and change over time. The course provides six themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: humans and the environment, cultural developments and interactions, governance, economic systems, social interactions and organization, and technology and innovation. Students also learn to write intentionally to score on AP specific rubrics and to develop test taking methods of reducing selections for multiple choice. These skills are essential to narrowing the scope of World History knowledge to address pertinent questions and relevant key words in prompts to help higher performance on the exam.
courses.prerequisites: World History 9
courses.notes: Recommended a grade of 85 or higher in World History 9 or Teacher recommendation.

courses.description: US History focuses on in-depth analysis of major themes of the US history era including economic, social and political history, foreign and domestic policy, as well as race, ethnicity, gender and sexuality. The course will primarily take a historical lens, though we will spend significant time exploring civics and geography as well. Woven through it all is the development of inquiry skills; building in all of us the skills and ability to ask questions of the world around us, develop arguments and analyze the arguments of others. The course is designed such that as we progress, more freedom is given to students to develop their own questions, though there may be a guiding topic or purpose.
courses.prerequisites: World History 10 or AP World History

courses.description: In AP U.S. History, students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods from approximately 1491 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical connections; and utilizing reasoning about comparison, causation, and continuity and change. The course also provides eight themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: American and national identity; work, exchange, and technology; geography and the environment; migration and settlement; politics and power; America in the world; American and regional culture; and social structures.
courses.prerequisites: World History 10 or AP World History
courses.notes: Recommended a grade of 85 or higher in AP World History or World History 10 or Teacher recommendation.

courses.description: This course will explore the ideas, theories, and methods of the scientific study of behavior and mental processes. Students will examine the concepts of psychology through reading and discussion and will analyze data from psychological research studies. Students will connect psychological concepts and theories to real-life scenarios and understand and interpret data. Through inquiry and critical thinking students will gain insight and awareness of human development, emotion and motivation, how we acquire knowledge, how our mind perceives and processes the world, and how we are all affected by where and how we live.
courses.prerequisites: World History 10 or AP World History
courses.notes: Recommended a grade of 85 or higher in AP World History or World History 10 or teacher recommendation.

courses.course_name: Current Issues and World Affairs I
courses.description: In this course, we will be exploring the current state of the globe on a variety of flexible topics based on what is presently happening in the nation and world at large. From wars, natural disasters, and social injustices to cultural developments, elections, and technology, the course will discuss which topics are presently developing in our local and global communities. Within the structure of the course, we will focus on several key, reoccurring themes, including political systems in action, international relations and cultures, local and global economies at work, and connecting local and global issues. There will also be a primary focus on how we obtain and utilize a variety of news information. This will involve exploring how to best research and comprehending biases from certain sources and perspectives and how that informs views. To be successful in this course, students will have an interest in discussing and analyzing developments in our modern world while also looking to connect world history and future predictions for how events develop. Our main academic focuses will include discussion, reflection, and research, so students should be ready to work self-sufficiently and consider their personal perspective. This course will be invaluable for anyone looking to discuss and explore what is currently happening as well as knowing how to best obtain and approach information. Students may take CIWA II, III, & IV as the topics discussed change based on student interest and context.
courses.prerequisites: World History 10 or AP World History

courses.description: In this course, students will explore key economic concepts like GDP, inflation, unemployment, tax policy and economic growth. They'll examine how government policies, such as fiscal and monetary actions, affect national economies and individuals' lives. Through real-world examples and current events, students will develop a deeper understanding of economic systems, global trade, and the role of central banks. This course helps students build critical thinking skills while exploring the major forces shaping today's global economy.
courses.prerequisites: World History 9

courses.description: This course is designed for students to gain a greater understanding of money and its role in their lives and futures. The course will focus on how saving, borrowing, and investing works, the magic of compounding interest, personal finances and the consumer decision-making process. Following that, we will learn about a variety of career fields and individual jobs using widely available databases of employment and salaries, job shadowing assignments, and by hosting regular professional guest speakers. This course is essential for anyone expecting to earn a living in the future.
courses.prerequisites: World History 9

courses.description: In this course, students will study the fundamental principles that govern individual markets, businesses, and consumer behavior. Topics include supply and demand, market structures, pricing strategies, and the government’s role in regulating markets. Students will also explore how factors such as incentives, competition, and resource allocation affect decision-making for consumers and producers. Through real-world examples and case studies, students will develop a deeper understanding of how economic forces shape everyday choices and the functioning of local and global markets.
courses.prerequisites: World History 9

courses.description: State and Local Government introduces the structure, function and procedures for decision making at the national, state and local level with an emphasis on state and local government. This course will cultivate the knowledge, skills and dispositions in students to be engaged community members invested in the common good, community service and the issues in which they are individually invested.
courses.prerequisites: Completion or concurrent enrollment of US History or AP US History

courses.description: This course is to provide students time to build on foundational mathematics skills. Topics include basic operations, fractions, factoring, percentages, solving equations, probability, and measurement. The goal of this course is to create strong mathematical understanding in order to move on to Algebra.

In Pre-Algebra, students will work to strengthen their mathematical foundations in order to be better prepared for Algebra I. Students will work on number sense, rates and ratios, and integer operations and rational numbers. These units will work to improve arithmetic skills before moving on to graphing proportional relationships, equivalent expressions and equations, and linear relationships. Pre-Algebra spends time on these algebraic skills in order to begin getting students comfortable with the abstraction that is required in Algebra I.

This course introduces many of the fundamental building blocks of high school mathematics. The topics of study will include the number system, simplifying expressions, solving and manipulating equations, linear equations, systems of linear equations, understanding and building functions, and manipulating polynomials and quadratics. Students will also spend time building connections between algebra topics and data and statistics. Students will learn to visually represent data and analyze their findings. In this course students will learn logical reasoning and problem solving skills that will be applicable in all future math courses.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of 8th grade math and/or Pre-Algebra.

courses.description: This course introduces the student to the second major field of mathematics. The study of geometric figures and their properties is axiomatically developed using definitions, postulates and theorems. Course content includes the study of geometric relationships in both two and three dimensions and utilizes the coordinate system to relate geometric concepts to the student’s background in algebra.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1

courses.description: This is a course designed for students to continue learning concepts from Algebra 1 and to introduce new concepts in Algebra 2. The major subjects covered in this course are Functions, Linear Functions, Quadratic Functions, and various other Functions, including Polynomials. Within each Function, we will cover writing equations, solving equations and graphing. We will learn how to apply different functions to represent different real-world scenarios.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Geometry

courses.description: This course is an extension of Algebra I. The course is designed to give more of an understanding of our number system and the use of axioms in mathematical manipulation. The major subjects covered are quadratics, polynomials, set theory, identities, rational expressions, relations and functions, logarithms, trigonometry, and statistics and probability.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I and Geometry; Geometry may be taken concurrently

courses.description: This course is intended for those students with a strong aptitude in mathematics or for those who want to prepare for calculus and other advanced math and science courses. The first semester deals with an extension of algebra, polynomial functions, rational functions, exponential functions, and logarithms. The second semester consists of a comprehensive study of trigonometry including analytical trigonometry.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra II and Geometry

courses.description: This course is open to those students with a strong record of mathematics achievement. The course covers a review of coordinate geometry and elementary functions and is then followed by a discussion on limits, a study of the derivative and applications, and the integral and applications. Graphing technology is used to aid learning. Science and business uses of calculus are included.
courses.prerequisites: PreCalculus

courses.description: This is a fast-paced college level course designed to prepare students for the AP Examination in Mathematics, Calculus AB exam. The course provides excellent preparation for college mathematics, and students who do well on the AP Exam can receive up to 4 credits at the college they attend. The course covers functions and graphs, including algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions, and the calculation of limits, as well as topics in differential and integral calculus. Science and business uses of calculus are included.
courses.prerequisites: Pre-Calculus or Calculus

courses.description: This half-year course presents an introduction to basic statistical methods that can prepare students to take AP Statistics, if they choose, or for a college level statistics course. The course will cover topics such as distributions and graphical representations and measures of central tendency and variability, normal distribution, scatter plots, experimental design, frequency tables, and probability rules.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Geometry; May be taken with Algebra II
courses.offering_note: Math electives: offering based on demand (per pathways chart, p.25)

courses.description: The purpose of this course is to introduce students to the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data. Students are exposed to four broad conceptual themes: · Exploring Data: Describing patterns and departures from patterns · Sampling and Experimentation: Planning and conducting a study · Anticipated Patterns: Exploring random phenomena using probability and simulation · Statistical Inference: Estimating population parameters and testing hypotheses AP Students will be expected to take quizzes and tests throughout the courses based on the format of the actual AP stats exam (i.e. multiple choice and long answer problems). You must have a T1-84 series calculator for both Statistics and AP Statistics.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra II OR Foundations of Algebra II and Statistics

courses.description: This one semester course will combine math and psychology to answer the overarching question: How do humans make decisions, and what types of errors take place? Students will simulate real-world game shows, and delve into different types of cognitive biases. Project-based learning will be emphasized throughout the course.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Geometry; may be taken with Foundations of Algebra II or Algebra II
courses.offering_note: Math electives: offering based on demand (per pathways chart, p.25)

courses.description: This is a class designed to provide support and instruction to students who are developing their math skills. Students access this course through SHS faculty recommendation. This class can be taken multiple times, for up to 1 total math credit. Additional credits will be awarded as elective credit only.
courses.prerequisites: Students are not able to individually register for this course but will be scheduled for the course based upon teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Students are not able to individually register; scheduled by teacher recommendation.

courses.description: Concert band is a musical organization, which offers instruction and playing experience for players of woodwind, brass and percussion instruments for grades 9-12. The band represents the school at various concerts and other events annually. The course includes the study of music literature through performance, developing skills in interpretation, phrasing, intonation, balance, together with the understanding of various forms and styles. Students are eligible for participation in auditioning for various festivals including the Northeastern Vermont District Music Festival and Vermont All-State Music Festival. If a student is enrolled in both band and chorus they will receive .5 band credit and .5 chorus credit.
courses.notes: Credit .5 or 1 as printed.

courses.description: This ensemble is designed for students who enjoy singing and would like to learn more about music and vocal technique. In the course students will perform songs in three- and four-part harmony, learn basic music notation related to interpreting choral music, and develop skits in interpretation, phrasing, intonation, balance and performance. Concert selections will include music from a wide variety of cultural and historical genres. Chorus members are eligible to participate in area music festivals including the Northeastern VT District Music Festival and the Vermont All-State Music Festival. If a student is enrolled in both band and chorus they will receive .5 band credit and .5 chorus credit.
courses.notes: Credit .5 or 1 as printed.

courses.description: From rock to folk, funk to pop, the guitar is a versatile instrument that lets artists across the world express themselves through music. In this course, we’ll be learning about the fundamental techniques needed to play the guitar as well as some related skills like music theory and songwriting.

Students who participate in the high school musical will engage in a wide variety of skills and activities related to musical theater. Students participating as actors on stage will hone skills relating to acting, dancing, singing, and storytelling in the musical theater style. Students participating on the technical crews will work in a variety of areas, including stage managing, backstage tech crew, lighting and sound design, props, art design, hair and makeup design, photography, and playing in the live pit band. The musical is a great chance for any student to be part of theatrical production and experience the performing arts. This is not a course that students select as part of their course registration process but sign up for separately through the music department. A student may earn up to .5 credits total, each experience is worth .25 credits to meet the district/state distribution requirement for Arts in a manner other than the traditional classroom experience. Students who participate in the musical are eligible for the Alternative Arts credit and the student is responsible for completing the alternative arts form. Not eligible for community service.
courses.fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Arts Credit; to meet the district/state distribution requirement for Arts in a manner other than the traditional classroom experience (up to .5 credits total)
courses.notes: program; not selected during course registration; signed up for separately through the music department; each experience worth .25 credits; alternative arts form required

courses.description: How do music makers capture their ideas in recorded form for us to enjoy over our speakers or headphones? In this course, students will learn about the basics of music production in this introductory course. Students will listen to and analyze landmark records, learn the basics of how to operate a digital audio workstation (DAW), and try their hand at creating their own original music. This course is open to anyone with a genuine curiosity about the process of creating recorded music. No previous musical experience is required!

courses.course_name: Music History - A Study of The Human Affinity For Sound
courses.description: An ancient human hit a hollow log with a stick. One thing led to another, and The Beatles released Abby Road. In this course, students will join Mr. Gagnon on a journey throughout the entirety of human history through the vehicle of music, from the first known musical compositions, to the classical masters, to the birth of hip-hop, to the new music that’s being written and performed today. Students in this course will spend time listening to music, discussing the technical aspects and historical context of important artists, songs, and styles, and doing whatever else Mr. Gagnon thinks would be fun. No previous musical experience is required!

Students will participate in a variety of games in teams of 3-12 players. Schedules, matchups, Tournaments, playoffs, brackets, and standings can all be used as students work with their team to succeed. Students will gain knowledge of each game including the rules and developing the understanding to referee games. Students that value a team environment will do well in this class. The games might include soccer, basketball, volleyball, wiffleball, flag football, ultimate frisbee, floor hockey, thoukball, handball, and dodgeball.

Students will participate individually or with a partner in many activities. Students who can motivate themselves and prefer to play alone will enjoy this class. Students will learn the rules for many games and also participate in some tournaments. Activities are likely based on student interest but could include tennis, pickleball, badminton, spikeball, kanjam, washers, cornhole, bocce, dance, yoga,track and field, orienteering, and outdoor activities.

Students that want to make improvements to their physical and mental health will succeed in this class. Utilizing the weight room, the outdoor track, and other PE facilities, students will spend class time learning techniques, designing workout plans, and exercising in a way to meet their goal. Students will work out almost every day with some occasional game time based on the interests of the class.

The Stowe School Board approved the earning of up to .5 credits to meet the graduation requirement for physical education, in a manner other than the traditional classroom experience. Students can receive .25 credit per a sports season they participate in. Students can earn up to .5 credit total of ALT PE credit toward graduation. To meet SHS graduation requirements students must have a total of 1 PE credit. The student can earn the remaining PE credit through SHS physical education courses. Students are responsible for completing the Alt PE form. Students are required to take one physical education course (one semester) and earn .5 credit before they can access alternative PE credit. This cannot be used to replace Health Education.
courses.prerequisites: Students must complete the Alt. PE form
courses.fulfills_text: Credit Type: Physical Education; to meet the graduation requirement for physical education, in a manner other than the traditional classroom experience (up to .5 credit)
courses.notes: program; .25 credit per sports season; Alt. PE form required

courses.description: This course's foundation is rooted in the National Health Education Standards. Students will work towards developing skills of effective communication, goal setting, analyzing influences, accessing valid and reliable information, and demonstrating health enhancing practices. Students will aim towards demonstrating proficiency in these health skills through exploration of content themes including mental and emotional health, substance use prevention, human sexuality, violence and injury prevention, and public health. By completion of the course students should demonstrate proficiency for multiple indicators identified by the Vermont Portrait of a Graduate for Health Education: learner agency, global citizenship, academic proficiency, communication, critical thinking and problem solving, and well-being.

Culture Through Cuisine class aims to accomplish three main things. The first is teaching students nutrition through cooking healthy meals from scratch. The meals we create come from various cultures throughout the world. The second is to build the skills to make conscious food choices at the individual, societal, and environmental level. The course explores food justice concepts and examines food injustices occurring in our world in order to impact food choices. Finally the course examines personal identity and culture through exploration of the intersectionality of food and culture. Students will examine social determinants of health and how those impact our food choices, as well as work towards developing a personal food identity project. Students will be assessed on their core knowledge of nutrition, the ability to practice safe and healthy practices while cooking and in the kitchen, as well as advocacy.
courses.prerequisites: Health

courses.description: Earth Science is designed as a class to study phenomena at various scales across natural and human systems. During this course students will be expected to develop written communication skills to construct evidence-based arguments. As for analysis students will have to accurately develop models and perform manipulations to models to then explain scientific phenomena. Students will also be working on investigative skills that focus on error analysis centralized around human error while measuring data manually. As for content Earth Science includes understanding the existence of our universe (the Big Bang), Earth’s history and its age, Earth’s systems (plate tectonics, feature formation, weathering, & erosion), the development of weather and climate change, and studying how humans alter the Earth and how to better sustain our resources (human sustainability).

Biology, which students may take after successful completion of 9th grade Earth Science, utilizes investigations and independent research to introduce life science concepts and advance scientific skills. Investigations will emphasize analyzing patterns in data to identify human and systematic error. Students will independently record and manipulate data using digital sensors, tools and software. Data analysis will emphasize the creation and manipulation of models, and applying mathematical and statistical computations to determine accuracy, precision, and significance. Analysis and reasoning of these experiments will be communicated through formal lab reports and in-class tests. Major areas of content will focus on investigating ecological interdependence, modeling the structural and functional relationships of biomolecules and cells, investigating energetic enzymatic systems within organisms, modeling and analyzing genetic inheritance and expression, and finally modeling and analyzing evolutionary pressures and changes.
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science

courses.description: Chemistry, which students may take after successful completion of 10th grade Biology, uses an understanding of energy and forces at atomic and subatomic scales to understand our world. Investigations will develop students' chemistry-related lab skills and ability to work quantitatively with the precision necessary to be effective chemists. Analysis will build off of 10th grade skills while increasing student’s use of quantitative models and their ability to connect abstract models to fundamental scientific laws and theories. Major topics of study include gas laws, matter and energy, atomic structure, chemical bonding, mathematics of chemistry, and kinetics and equilibrium.
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science and Biology

courses.description: This course will cover in detail the following topics: graphical analysis, measurement, analytical methods, Newtonian Mechanics (linear motion, work energy, power and momentum), electrostatics, basic DC electric circuits, and magnetism. Students will have the opportunity to use digital sensors (motion sensors, photogate timers, smart pulley timers, force sensors, current, voltage, and resistance sensors) and associated software in order to study the topics mentioned above. The course is organized around experiments, inquiry projects and engineering projects performed in class.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra II, Earth Science, and Biology

courses.description: Advanced Placement Biology, offered at the high school level, is designed to reflect as closely as possible a freshman-level biology course in college. Students enrolled in this course will be expected to take the AP Examination in mid-May for advanced placement credit in college. Topics to be covered include biochemistry, cellular biology, molecular biology, molecular genetics, Mendelian genetics, evolution, taxonomy, and microbiology, the diverse characteristics of plants and animals and ecology. Laboratories will be an integral part of each of these topics. Students will be expected to do a great deal of independent study. The course will terminate by allowing students several weeks to study and work on a project of their choosing. This class will next be offered in 2027-2028
courses.prerequisites: Biology and Earth Science. Completion or current enrollment in Algebra II. Can be taken concurrently with Chemistry or Physics.
courses.offering_note: This class will next be offered in 2027-2028 (not offered 2026-27)
courses.notes: Recommended a grade of 85 in either Biology or Chemistry

courses.description: This fast-paced course is designed to prepare students for the AP exam in Environmental Science and the potential for college credit. Through this course, students will learn the scientific principles, concepts, and methodologies required to understand the interrelationship of the natural world, to identify and analyze environmental problems both natural and human made, to evaluate the relative risks associated with these problems, and to examine alternative solutions for resolving and/or preventing them. This class will be offered in 2026-2027
courses.prerequisites: Biology and Earth Science. Completion or current enrollment in Algebra II. Can be taken concurrently with Chemistry or Physics.
courses.offering_note: This class will be offered in 2026-2027
courses.notes: Recommended a grade of 85 in Biology or Chemistry

courses.description: Advanced Placement Physics 1, is the equivalent to a first-semester college course in algebra-based physics. The course covers Newtonian mechanics (including rotational dynamics and angular momentum); work, energy, and power; and fluids. The ability to develop and use physics knowledge by applying it to the practice of scientific inquiry and reasoning is at the heart of this physics course. Students will construct knowledge through experimenting, analyzing, making conjectures and arguments, and solving problems in a collaborative setting throughout the course. Students enrolled in this course will be expected to take the AP examination in mid-May for advanced placement credit in college. After the exam, students will have several weeks to work on an engineering design task of their choosing.
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science, Biology, and Algebra II.

courses.description: Food science is focused on scientific phenomena and their chemical interactions. The molecules the course studies are salts, fats, carbohydrates, and proteins. Students will learn about the structure of each molecule, its interactions,why we consume them, and how they can be manipulated to achieve desired culinary outcomes. Students should have strong inquiry skills, ability to conduct experiments, data analysis, modeling, and scientific writing. Students should expect attendance to be important as the class will have frequent labs, with heavy emphasis on methods, data collection, modeling, and conclusions.
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science

courses.description: This class will examine the physiology, anatomy, and biochemistry of the human body, focusing on healthy minds and bodies. The course will be organized around the 11 body systems and their structure and function. Students should be advanced in their inquiry skills, ability to conduct investigations, data analysis, modeling, and scientific writing. Various units will pair body systems together to test how they impact one another like how the use of the muscular system impacts one's cardiovascular endurance. This class will include many self-designed inquiry labs that will require students to use peer-published scientific studies to understand recent discoveries in the field of physiology to help support their own conclusions. A strong science background is encouraged for those who enjoy both content and investigations.
courses.prerequisites: Biology

courses.description: In this semester long course students will have the opportunity to follow their own interest in learning how things work. Participants will use multiple strategies depending on interest and the object involved including: reading and research, inquiry investigations, organized disassembling of objects, and building of analogs using available materials. Interested in music? Here’s your chance to study the science of instruments. Use sound sensors to measure and visualize sound waves and develop an Inquiry investigation. Try your hand at building your own instruments. Have you wondered how motors and generators work? Take one apart, study electromagnetism and learn to build a simple one of your own. Can you maximize its torque? If you’re curious about an object there are lots to learn. This course is well suited to motivated independent students.

S.T.E.A.M. It is a semester-long course that exposes students to the many intersections between Science, Technology, Engineering, Art/Design, and Math. During the course of the semester, students explore these fields through hands-on project-based designs, design challenges, engaging text, and other media. This course is designed to introduce students to new tools and materials, and allows for skills acquisition and gain proficiency through practice. Projects range from creating 3D models using SketchUp and TinkerCAD and a 3D printer, to DC electronics circuitry, and soldering. Students should be prepared to be introduced to and use power and hand tools, design objects using both pencil/paper and CAD software, research and then communicate solutions to common problems, and build prototypes of everything from 3D printed game pieces, to small wooden boxes, to working Bluetooth enabled stereo speakers. Other topics include: · Coding/Computer Programming · Arduino Microcontrollers/Physical Computing · Working Machines/Robotics

S.T.E.A.M. II, III, IV are advanced, project-driven courses designed to expand on the skills and concepts introduced in S.T.E.A.M. I. In these semester-long classes, students will deepen their understanding of the intersections between Science, Technology, Engineering, Art/Design, and Math through more complex and interdisciplinary challenges. Building upon prior knowledge, students will engage in collaborative projects that integrate advanced CAD design, robotics, programming, and circuit building. Throughout these courses, students will work on multi-step projects, where they will prototype, test, and refine solutions to real-world problems. They will use cutting-edge tools such as CNC machines, advanced 3D modeling software, and microcontroller platforms (e.g., Raspberry Pi) to create functional, innovative designs. Students will also delve into more advanced coding techniques, utilizing languages such as Python and C++ to control more sophisticated systems.

S.T.E.A.M. II, III, IV are advanced, project-driven courses designed to expand on the skills and concepts introduced in S.T.E.A.M. I. In these semester-long classes, students will deepen their understanding of the intersections between Science, Technology, Engineering, Art/Design, and Math through more complex and interdisciplinary challenges. Building upon prior knowledge, students will engage in collaborative projects that integrate advanced CAD design, robotics, programming, and circuit building. Throughout these courses, students will work on multi-step projects, where they will prototype, test, and refine solutions to real-world problems. They will use cutting-edge tools such as CNC machines, advanced 3D modeling software, and microcontroller platforms (e.g., Raspberry Pi) to create functional, innovative designs. Students will also delve into more advanced coding techniques, utilizing languages such as Python and C++ to control more sophisticated systems.

S.T.E.A.M. II, III, IV are advanced, project-driven courses designed to expand on the skills and concepts introduced in S.T.E.A.M. I. In these semester-long classes, students will deepen their understanding of the intersections between Science, Technology, Engineering, Art/Design, and Math through more complex and interdisciplinary challenges. Building upon prior knowledge, students will engage in collaborative projects that integrate advanced CAD design, robotics, programming, and circuit building. Throughout these courses, students will work on multi-step projects, where they will prototype, test, and refine solutions to real-world problems. They will use cutting-edge tools such as CNC machines, advanced 3D modeling software, and microcontroller platforms (e.g., Raspberry Pi) to create functional, innovative designs. Students will also delve into more advanced coding techniques, utilizing languages such as Python and C++ to control more sophisticated systems.

This introductory course teaches the foundations of programming with emphasis on helping students understand basic Javascript logic and syntax. Students will learn basic command structure, input/output function, and simple code-based image generation. By the end of the course, students will be able to independently code their own basic Javascript programs. An interest in coding is recommended but no prior coding knowledge is required.

This course is a continuation of Introduction to Coding I and builds on learning by adding sophistication to prior learning as well as introducing more advanced Javascript coding concepts/structures. By the end of this course, the goal is each student to recreate a simplified version of one of several well-known video games. The scope of material covered in Coding I & II is equivalent to a semester-long college-level course.
courses.prerequisites: Coding I

courses.description: This course provides students with a hands-on introduction to the exciting field of Robotics. Through a combination of theoretical learning and practical application, students will explore the fundamentals of robotics, including mechanical design, electronics, programming, and problem-solving. Using industry-standard hardware and software, students will work both individually and in teams to design, build, and program their own robots to complete various challenges and tasks. Topics covered will include: 1. Introduction to Robotics: History, applications, and current trends 2. Mechanical Design: Basics of robot chassis, joints, and mechanisms 3. Electronics: Understanding sensors, actuators, and microcontrollers 4. Programming: Introduction to coding languages such as Python and C++ for robot control 5. Sensors and Feedback: Utilizing sensors for navigation, object detection, and feedback control 6. Control Systems: PID control, feedback loops, and tuning 7. Robot Platforms: Exploring different types of robots such as wheeled, legged, and aerial 8. Applications: Real-world examples of robotics in industry, healthcare, and beyond 9. Team Projects: Collaborative design and implementation of robotic systems to solve specific challenges 10. Ethical and Societal Implications: Discussions on the impact of robotics on society, ethics, and responsible innovation

French I is an introductory course that emphasizes fundamental understanding of vocabulary, structures, and culture of the francophone world. The course aims to build novice communication skills across the modalities of speaking, writing, reading and listening. The course also includes cultural projects that are designed to build student knowledge of the people and customs of the French-speaking world.

This course is designed to develop French proficiency in communication at the intermediate level. New verb tenses are introduced along with other grammar concepts aimed at creating sentences that are more complex. Students also continue to explore different aspects of French culture and new vocabulary through the different modalities of speaking, reading, writing and listening.
courses.prerequisites: French I or 8th grade French with teacher recommendation

courses.description: In French III, students expand their capacity to communicate in the French by adding more complex verb tenses and grammar structures to their repertoire. This allows the student to generate more of his/her own meaning in a greater range of contexts. Vocabulary study continues to focus on relevant and authentic situations but also incorporates areas of student interest. In addition to embedding cultural knowledge into communication activities, French III offers stand-alone thematic units on cultural topics of the francophone world. At this level, students also begin to read more passage-length texts than in previous levels.
courses.prerequisites: French II

courses.description: In French IV, students enter the advanced level of French study. This course tackles the more complex verb tenses and grammar structures necessary to comprehend and communicate in more challenging language situations. This course requires students to read and write more substantive pieces in the target language. Classroom conversations are more sustained than in previous levels and require students to discuss topics from class readings. Readings include works of French literature as well as current events and contemporary media articles.
courses.prerequisites: French III

courses.description: French V represents an advanced opportunity for students who desire to increase the authenticity and fluency of their communication. This course offers contemporary materials, activities, and perspectives that prepare students to engage confidently and knowledgeably in francophone regions near and far. In addition to focusing on fluency and contemporary expression, the course also includes reading that is more extensive and writing activities thatResemble the demands of intermediate college-level literature and culture courses. This is a full-immersion class.
courses.prerequisites: French IV

courses.description: This is an introduction to Spanish class. We will use a variety of strategies to provide students with the opportunity to acquire the Spanish language and learn about the culture of Spanish speaking countries. The goal is to understand, speak, read and write at beginner level.

Students will continue to develop comprehension skills and acquire high frequency Spanish structures. Throughout the course, we will read short stories and novels that make connections to relevant world events. We will also listen to songs and watch videos on a variety of topics. Discussions in class will be based on the student's interests as well themes that arise from our reading and listening activities.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish I or 8th grade Spanish with teacher recommendation

courses.description: This course is a continuation of Spanish II, where more advanced vocabulary and structures are introduced through discussions, pictures, videos and songs. We will again read short stories and leveled readers to connect to Spanish culture and language.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish II

courses.description: This course will include the study of art/beauty, family and community, global challenges, science and technology, and contemporary life. We will use songs. videos, short texts and books to dive into all those themes while at the same time acquire more Spanish.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish III

courses.description: This course is designed to increase students' communication in the target language both written and spoken. We will continue to explore the themes we started in Spanish IV going deeper in our discussions as students' acquisition of Spanish improves. As in previous classes, we will be watching videos, learning songs, reading short stories and texts as well as books.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish IV

courses.description: Independent Study experiences provide students the chance for a highly personalized investigation and analysis of a topic of interest outside of the regular SHS curriculum. Only in exceptional cases will Independent Studies cover the same content/proficiencies as a course already offered in the SHS Program of Studies. However, in these cases, the independent study will act as an extension or “deeper dive” into proficiencies already covered in an SHS course the student has taken previously. All independent study experiences must be advised by a current SHS employed/licensed faculty. Therefore, it is the decision of the faculty member if they will act as an advisor for an independent study. Students planning to apply for an independent study must complete all forms BEFORE the proposed first day of the study. If a student is interested in an independent study option, they will need to meet with their school counselor. All approved and completed Independent Study experiences, supported by a SHS faculty member, will appear on the SHS transcript and the proficiency earned will be factored into the SHS GPA. * Students being tutored outside of school by persons not employed by the district do not earn credit or a grade and therefore, no tutoring experience will appear on the transcript. Students may be paired with a community mentor to act as an additional guide for the independent study.
courses.notes: program; All approved and completed Independent Study experiences, supported by a SHS faculty member, will appear on the SHS transcript

courses.description: The SHINE program offers students differing levels of exposure to the world of work, depending on their interests. Possibilities include: ● Informational interviews with professionals in a career field of interest to the student ● Worksite visits ● Interview skills and practice ● Resume development ● Local employment and Community Service opportunities In addition to the above experiences are open to Juniors and Seniors. The SHINE coordinator also designs and manages formal internships for students. Students will work with the SHINE coordinator on pre-internship activities and preparation, and then be paired with a mentor in the greater Stowe community in the career field of their choice. The student is expected to complete 40 hours of work either remotely or at the internship site (schedule to be determined by the mentor and student, could be school hours, after school, weekends, etc.) Students will be assessed using LSUU Mission Related Goals and specific work site skills. This is a flexible, fantastic opportunity for students to get professional experience and school credit at the same time. Students enrolled in SHINE will not meet as a class, but there will be occasional cohort meetings and regularly scheduled meetings with the SHINE coordinator. Prerequisites: Demonstrate proficiency in Scholarly Habits or by permission of instructor. Semester Course for .5 credit and students may be extended/repeated for other internship opportunities.

courses.description: Flexible Pathways is a course provided by another high school accredited program (VTVLC, BYU). If a student is planning to enroll in a flexible pathways course, the Flexible Pathways Form must be completed BEFORE the first day of class . This form contains important information and considerations to review before official enrollment. All approved and completed flexible pathways courses will appear on the SHS transcript, noted in the flexible pathways section. The grade earned will not be factored into the SHS GPA. Flexible pathways courses are intended to supplement, not replace, course offerings at Stowe High School. Virtual offerings will not be counted as credit that replace required courses offered by the school unless special circumstances apply that require a student to take virtual coursework (e.g., medical need).
